title: Rearranging Formulas
summary:
Rearranging a formula — 'making a different letter the subject' — is the single most useful algebra skill in energy science, because the textbook almost never gives you the equation in the form you need. The good news: it runs on **one rule** and a short list of **inverse operations**, applied patiently.

**The golden rule:** an equation is a balance. *Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.* If you add 5 on the left, add 5 on the right; if you divide the left by $t$, divide the *whole* right by $t$. Do that and the equality stays true — always.

**The strategy: peel the onion.** To isolate a variable, undo the operations wrapped around it **in reverse order** — the opposite order to BIDMAS. Look at everything done *to* your target variable, then strip it away one layer at a time using the inverse operation. The inverses you need: addition ↔ subtraction, multiplication ↔ division, square ↔ square root, and (later) exponential ↔ logarithm.

**Scenario 1 — something added or subtracted.** To make $a$ the subject of $v = u + at$: the $at$ term is *added*, so subtract it from both sides, $v - u = at$; then $a$ is *multiplied* by $t$, so divide both sides by $t$: $$a = \frac{v - u}{t}.$$ Notice you subtract first, divide second — reverse BIDMAS.

**Scenario 2 — the variable is multiplied or divided.** For density $\rho = m/V$, to get $m$: $m$ is divided by $V$, so multiply both sides by $V$, giving $m = \rho V$. To get $V$ instead, it's trickier because $V$ is *underneath*. Multiply both sides by $V$ first ($\rho V = m$), then divide by $\rho$: $$V = \frac{m}{\rho}.$$ **Rule of thumb: if your variable is in the denominator, multiply both sides by it to lift it up, then isolate.**

**Scenario 3 — the variable is squared (or under a root).** For $A = \pi r^2$, to get $r$: divide by $\pi$ ($A/\pi = r^2$), then take the square root of both sides: $$r = \sqrt{\tfrac{A}{\pi}}.$$ Square and square-root are inverses, so they cancel. (In pure maths a square root is $\pm$; for a physical quantity like a radius you keep the positive root.) If instead the variable is *under* a root, do the opposite — **square both sides** to remove the root.

**Scenario 4 — the variable appears more than once / on both sides.** Collect it. To solve $5x - 3 = 2x + 9$: get all $x$ on one side (subtract $2x$): $3x - 3 = 9$; then the added/subtracted constant (add 3): $3x = 12$; then divide: $x = 4$. When the variable appears inside a bracket as a common factor, **factor it out** so it appears once, then divide.

**The universal recipe:** (1) identify your target letter; (2) list what's been done to it; (3) undo those operations in reverse order, applying each step to *both whole sides*; (4) check by substituting numbers back in. With practice this becomes automatic — and every physics and thermodynamics formula in the rest of the app becomes something you can bend to your needs.

equations.name: Scenario: term added or subtracted
equations.useWhen: Your variable is part of a term that is added to or subtracted from something else. **Undo the +/− first** (subtract or add the same on both sides), then undo any ×/÷.
equations.note: Reverse-BIDMAS: deal with +/− before ×/÷ when *isolating*. Subtract the whole extra term from both sides.

equations.name: Scenario: variable in the denominator
rearrangements: \text{step 1: multiply both sides by } x \Rightarrow xy = a
equations.useWhen: The variable you want is *underneath* a fraction. Multiply both sides by it to bring it up to the top, then isolate as usual.
equations.note: Don't try to divide it out while it's in the denominator — lift it first with multiplication.

equations.name: Scenario: variable squared / under a root
equations.useWhen: The variable is squared (take the square root last) or sits under a root (square both sides last). Square and root are inverses and cancel.
equations.note: Strip the ×/÷ around it first, then apply the root/square to the *whole* other side. Keep the positive root for physical quantities.

equations.name: Scenario: variable on both sides
equations.latex: ax + b = cx + d \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{d - b}{a - c}
equations.useWhen: The unknown appears more than once. Gather every term containing it on one side, factor it out so it appears once, then divide by its coefficient.
equations.note: Moving a term across the '=' flips its sign. Factoring turns repeated $x$'s into a single $x$ you can divide away.

glossary.definition: The variable on its own, usually on the left, that the formula is solved for. 'Make $a$ the subject' = rearrange until $a =$ (everything else).
The operation that undoes another: + and − are inverses; × and ÷ are inverses; squaring and square-rooting are inverses; exponentials and logs are inverses.
Whatever you do to one side of an equation you must do to the other, so the two sides stay equal. The basis of every legal rearrangement step.
A part of an expression separated by + or − signs. In $u + at$, the terms are $u$ and $at$. You move whole terms across the equals sign.
The number multiplying a variable. In $3x$ the coefficient is 3; you remove it by dividing both sides by it.
Terms with the same variable part, which can be combined: $5x$ and $2x$ are like terms ($5x - 2x = 3x$); $5x$ and $5$ are not.
Writing a common factor outside a bracket: $ax - cx = x(a - c)$. Used to make a repeated variable appear only once so you can isolate it.
When isolating a variable you undo operations in the opposite order to BIDMAS — strip away +/− before ×/÷, and brackets/powers last.
Left-hand side and right-hand side of an equation. A step must be applied to the whole LHS and the whole RHS to stay valid.
For $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$, a shortcut giving $ad = bc$. It's really just multiplying both sides by $b$ and by $d$.

tips: **Apply every step to the *whole* side.** If you divide by $t$, divide *all* of the other side by $t$, not just one term. This is the No. 1 source of rearrangement errors.
**Undo in reverse order (reverse BIDMAS).** Peel off additions/subtractions first, then multiplications/divisions, then powers/roots last — the opposite of how you'd evaluate.
**If the variable is in the denominator, lift it first.** Multiply both sides by it to bring it to the top, *then* isolate. Don't fight it while it's underneath.
**Moving a term across '=' flips its sign;** moving a factor across becomes the inverse operation (× becomes ÷). Keep a clear before/after each line.
**Squared variable ⇒ square-root last; variable under a root ⇒ square last.** Do the ×/÷ tidying first, then apply the root or square to the entire other side.
**Always sanity-check by substituting numbers.** Put simple values into your rearranged formula and the original — if both give the same result, your rearrangement is right.
